newsitem.title: UK: UK beet crop on course, needs rain as pests emerge.
newsitem.headline: UK beet crop on course, needs rain as pests emerge.

text.p: Britain's 1997/98 sugar beet crop could benefit from more moisture after a dry start to plantings as it battles against the emergence of field pests, beet experts said on Friday.
Dry spells and frost affected this year's beets at the crop's critical germination stage, partially offsetting the advantage gained after planting was completed ahead of last year's programme.
But although Britain has seen some rains in the last two weeks, correcting the patchy emergence and beet development, still more was needed to create moisture reserves for the plant tap roots.
"It (the crop) is doing quite nicely, the rain in May evened off establishment and a lot of the crops that were slow to emerge are catching up," said an official at independent consultants ADAS.
This month's rains helped the crop get over earlier problems with mice destroying seeds lying in dry beds.
Around two weeks ago, some beet plants were showing as many as seven leaves while others were much smaller and only had two or three leaves, he said.
As far as disease is concerned, aphid catches have been fairly low so far, causing the forecast of virus yellows incidence to be low.
"There are one or two building up and I suspect we could go from a low forecast to a reasonably high forecast quite quickly," the ADAS official said.
In a recent bulletin, the industry-funded Broom's Barn research centre said while aphids had started to fly they were still fairly scarce on the ground.
Other pests reported have been pygmy beetles in Norfolk, an attack of leatherjackets in some west Midlands fields and fresh weed emergence on light soils.
Isolated plants with downy mildew had been at various sites in north Norfolk but the yield effect should be minimal, it said.
The driest start to the year since 1929 in Britain was followed by showery weather for much of May and more showers are predicted to mid-June.
Water industry sources have said that although the wet weather is solving immediate soil and plant moisture problems, it will not be enough to solve longer term groundwater supply worries.
"The size of the plants at the moment is such that the water demand is not too high," the official said.
"But it is hot and it is dry and I would have thought that if this weather continues for a week it'll start slowing down the crop but it's okay at the moment."

According to the 24-hour forecast from Britain's Meteorological Office, most parts should see dry and sunny weather. But it would be cooler towards coasts and especially in the east where patchy low cloud or fog was likely.
